title: Traffic-related air pollution and respiratory symptoms in children living along trunk roads in Chiba Prefecture, Japan.
ehr_evidence: In the first and fourth surveys, a standard respiratory symptom questionnaire, the modified Japanese version of ATS-DLD-78-C, was sent through the schools to the parents of all subjects; exposure was estimated from ambient air monitoring stations, so the data source was a parent-completed survey, not an electronic health record.
summary: A four-year prospective cohort study of 2,506 schoolchildren aged 6-9 years in eight communities in Chiba Prefecture, Japan, examining the association between living near trunk roads with heavy traffic (traffic-related air pollution) and the prevalence and incidence of asthma and respiratory symptoms.
key_findings: The incidence of asthma significantly increased among boys living in roadside areas relative to rural areas (adjusted odds ratio = 3.77; 95% CI reflecting significance, p<0.05), even after adjustment for allergic history and indoor environment.

Among girls, the adjusted odds ratios for incidence of asthma were 4.03 for roadside and 1.74 for non-roadside areas relative to rural areas, but the roadside estimate was not statistically significant (95% CI included 1).
Among girls, testing for trends showed the prevalence of asthma increased significantly in the order of roadside > non-roadside > rural areas.
The incidence of wheeze did not differ in relation to the location of the home among either boys or girls.
A history of allergic diseases was associated with increased incidence of asthma in both sexes; maternal smoking and heating appliance type were not associated with any respiratory symptom.
captured_features: distance of home from trunk roads (<50 m roadside vs 50+ m vs rural)
ambient NO2 and suspended particulate matter (SPM) concentrations
daytime traffic density and proportion of heavy/diesel vehicles
history of allergic diseases (atopy, allergic rhinitis)
population: schoolchildren aged 6-9 years (first to third grade) in eight communities in Chiba Prefecture, Japan
exposure_domain: traffic-related air pollution (automobile exhaust, NO2, suspended particulate matter)
limitations: Loss to follow-up and selective migration (families with respiratory symptoms may have moved away), potentially underestimating the risk of living in roadside areas.
Exposure was estimated from ambient monitoring stations and distance from roads rather than individual personal exposure measurements.
Outcomes were self-reported by parents via questionnaire, risking misclassification.
Small number of children whose mothers smoked limited analysis of environmental tobacco smoke.
